summary: In this excerpt from Book 14, the narrator watches Ian give a talk at a public event. Ian ties the arrest at Wilson's house to a large surveillance-industrial complex, and the narrator feels their cause matters more than a personal mission to free the narrator's arrested brother. Back at the apartment, the narrator changes out of stage clothes and slips away from Sarah's crew. Monica, who is grading papers, shows the narrator a local TV news story about the protest and arrest, and reports that the narrator's parents want the narrator to move back home.
one_line: The narrator hears Ian link Wilson's arrest to mass surveillance, then returns home to find Monica upset over local TV coverage and parental pressure to move back.
key_facts: Ian spoke at a podium still dressed in his jeans and tweed jacket, with his glasses a little crooked and his hair uncombed.
Ian connected history, politics and passion, starting with the bust at Wilson’s house.
Ian tied the bust to a vast surveillance-industrial complex that had flourished for decades but was now operating on an almost unimaginably invasive scale.
The narrator felt that what they were doing was important in a different way after listening to Ian, and most of the audience wanted to help.
Wheeze texted the narrator to say the narrator's brother had been arrested.
After the talk, the narrator changed out of makeup and into their own clothes in the hotel suite.
Sarah was setting up her editing equipment and demanding Ian’s presentation slides while the narrator slipped out with a backpack.
The narrator hiked home without being stopped by any cops and reached the apartment well before the curfew.
Monica was deep into grading papers when the narrator came home.
Monica said, “I was on TV yesterday,” and her students had told her about it.
Monica said, “I wish I hadn’t worn that stupid hat.”
The local TV news story included a two-second shot of Sunday’s protest and about twenty seconds of Monica.
The reporter ended the story with the words “reporting from South Minneapolis,” as if he was in a war zone.
Monica said the narrator's parents were worried the narrator would get in trouble like Wilson and wanted the narrator to move back home.
The narrator answered, “This is my home.”
